headline: Approved a dog ordinance and policy that allow off-leash dogs only in listed areas.
summary: Staff presented draft findings for the Comprehensive Plan update and said about 246 people attended an open house. A Leonard Street resident spoke against a proposed path from Leddy Park to Leonard Street, and staff said the department will keep talking with neighbors.
decisions: Approved the dog ordinance and dog policy with the changes Lewis outlined, all in favor.
Approved the consent agenda, including the October meeting minutes, all in favor.

decision_titles: Dog ordinance (Appendix D, Section 7) and dog policy
October meeting minutes and consent agenda
plain_text:
Parks Commission Meeting 
November 10th, 2026 at 5:30pm 
645 Pine St., Front Conference Room & Zoom 
 
Staff in Attendance: Lewis, Sauve & O’Daniel 
Commissioners in Attendance: Lantieri, Boehm, Mobley, Etter, Davis, Bergmann & Mamo 
Public in Attendance: Joanne Hunt, Mark Barlow & Michael Miller 
 
Lantieri opened the meeting at 5:31pm by welcoming everyone.  
1. Agenda 
1.1 Motion to amend/adopt agenda 
Mobley made a motion to adopt the agenda, Boehm seconded.  
All were in favor, none opposed. 
2. Consent Agenda 
2.1 October Meeting Minutes 
Boehm made a motion to adopt the consent agenda, Bergmann seconded. 
All were in favor, none opposed.  
3. Public Forum – Time Certain, 6pm 
3.1 Verbal Comments 
Public forum was opened at 6pm. 
There were 3 members of the public present, 2 online and 1 in-person. 
Joanne Hunt, a Burlington resident who lives on Leonard Street, was present in-
person. She shared that she was surprised when a zoning sign went up near her 
house about a path connecting Leddy Park to Leonard Street, noting that she and 
multiple other neighbors were opposed to the path for a variety of reasons. She 
continued that she has since learned that some feedback from neighbors in 
support of this path was given, but she and the others opposed to it were not 
involved and did not know anything about it. Hunt then spoke to the permit 
appeal process, noting that she and her neighbors against the path have been 
going through that process and have a petition signed by 17 neighbors opposing 
it. She then shared her feelings of disappointment and discouragement at the 
lack of process, including getting neighbor input and notifying them. She 
continued by sharing that she has been in touch with Lewis directly and also 
Councilors Barlow and Carpenter, both of whom are supporting the Leonard 
Street constituents. She then shared that she’s not sure what else to do, noting 
that this will hugely impact neighbors on the street, especially the people living 
on the side of the street closer to Leddy Park who are the majority of neighbors 
against the path being put in. She said she understands why people on Leonard 
Street would like easier access to Leddy, but she shared that over the past five 
years, issues with the park like safety concerns, the noise, court lights, high
speed traffic on the road have all increased dramatically, all reasons why this 
path does not make sense to put in. Hunt then circled back to her concerns 
surrounding the lack of notification about this to the public, noting that with all 
of the different input opportunities about different plans over the years, it gets 
confusing. She continued that presentations at NPAs or elsewhere are just 
presentations, not opportunities for feedback. Hunt then shared an anecdote 
about she and one of her neighbors, who is for the path, both engaging with 
someone in a planning position of some sort who said not to worry and that 
there would be opportunities to give feedback before anything would happen, 
which Hunt noted did not happen. She then share that she was not sure how to 
proceed or if it could be walked back at one point, noting that Councilor Barlow 
was in touch with Lewis directly about setting a meeting to discuss this further.   
The 2 virtual attendees did not opt to speak when given the opportunity. 
Lantieri responded briefly that this is something that can be discussed more in 
the future, but noted the process and outreach that happened with the 2024 
Leddy Comprehensive Plan.  
Lewis shared that because it was a non-agenda item he did not want to have 
much conversation about it here but that the Department is committed to 
continuing to engage with the neighbors and City Councilors about this. 
Public forum was closed at 6:09pm. 
4. Deliberative Agenda 
4.1 Dog Ordinance (Appendix D, Section 7) 
Lantieri opened this item by reviewing what was discussed at the last meeting – 
the intent of the decisions and what would go into the ordinance vs. the policy, 
noting that Lewis started the policy and would be going through that at this 
meeting. 
Lewis noted that the changes to the ordinance have carried over from the last 
review and that there were no additional changes.  
Lantieri then pivoted the conversation towards the policy piece, noting that it 
seemed fairly straightforward, outlining the areas of the pilots as well as 
language about modification of the policy in other places. 
Lewis shared his screen for the group to review the draft policy. He shared that 
he had carried this over from previous conversations and the draft policy that 
had been created and noted that the City attorney had made some notes in the 
document. These included a question about a potential missing word, a question 
about whether or not there were plans for a specific time frame for the 
temporary off-leash dog areas, which Lewis noted his understanding was “until 
further notice”, and some thoughts on the commercial use of off-leash and 
fenced areas – including permitting process and approvals. Lewis continued that 
he added a section about the modification of the policy and the City attorney
added in that changes would need to be approved by the Parks Commission. He 
then opened it up to feedback and questions. 
Mamo asked for an example of a commercial use of an off-leash area.  
The group answered dog training, fundraising, or product promotions would be 
the most likely. 
Lantieri chimed in that that concept came from the last Director as a potential 
revenue generating concept.  
Etter shared his sentiment that there should be something in the policy that 
specifies that the off-leash areas noted in the policy are the only places where 
dogs can be off leash.  
There was general agreement about this and Lewis noted it in the draft 
document.  
Lantieri mentioned that he would be inclined to see a line about where the 
policy will be posted for public access.  
The group was generally in agreement. 
Lewis asked if the Commission would be okay not including that specifically in 
this policy right now, but instead have a broader conversation in the future 
about how to effectively communicate BPRW policies out to the public.  
Boehm thought this was a good idea – noting that a broad overview of how to 
interact with the policies would be better for the user and staff instead of 
putting it in individual policies and then potentially having to backtrack.  
Mobley asked that it be noted that the intention moving forward is for BPRW 
policies to be accessible for community members.   
There was general agreement on this from the group. 
Lantieri asked to review section 7C in the Ordinance, which is the piece about 
public information. He noted that section more or less covered what was needed 
to make sure there were measures in place to inform the community.  
Mamo asked about the reference to a pilot program at Oakledge, specifically. 
Lewis answered that Oakledge is noted as a permanent fenced off-leash location 
in a very outdated version of these documents but the only permanent off-leash 
beach in the ordinance is Texaco and Leddy is currently a pilot program. 
The group then discussed the term “year round” that was noted for some 
locations but not others, with Lewis offering to change the language to keep 
things consistent.  
Lantieri asked if anyone felt like anything was missing from this conversation at 
this point, noting that they could vote to approve the ordinance as is as well as 
the policy with the proposed changes made at this meeting if not.  
Boehm asked for clarification that the City attorney had reviewed the policy but 
had reviewed and signed off on the ordinance. 
Lewis confirmed. He shared his assumption that if these are both approved by 
this body that he would send the policy with the changes made to the City
attorney for a final review and then it would all go to City Council and then most 
likely the Ordinance Committee and PACC.  
Lantieri asked for confirmation that the only amendment that was actually made 
was the year round piece.  
Lewis reviewed the changes made – noting that they removed the areas of policy 
in the top section, added language about off-leash dogs only being allowed in 
the listed areas, removed “year round” from Starr Farm and the Urban Reserve, 
accepted the changes under section C about the approval process, including 
approval by the Commission.  
Boehm made a motion to adopt the dog ordinance, Appendix D, Section 7 and 
the referenced dog policy, including the changes that Lewis just outlined.  
Bergmann seconded.  
All were in favor, none opposed.  
4.2 Comprehensive Plan Update 
Sauve opened by sharing that she would be presenting the Commissioners with 
condensed data slides that staff were presented with last week. She continued 
by thanking the Commissioners who attended the Open House, noting that 
about 246 people attended in total and the general consensus so far is that they 
received a lot of good feedback during that. She shared that the vision and goals 
are still in draft mode and asked for help from Commissioners to help 
disseminate online information to those who weren’t able to attend soon once it 
is posted. Sauve continued that they are trying to coordinate a joint Commission 
meeting with this body, DPW’s Commission and the Planning Commission on 
December 17th and was hoping some BPRW Commissioners would be able to 
commit to attending.  
Multiple Commissioners confirmed they would be able to attend.  
There was a pause for the 6pm time certain public forum. 
Sauve then continued by sharing her screen to show a condensed version of the 
slides that depict the analysis of the Department and all of the work that is done, 
and noted that what she was about to show was an abbreviated version of the 
full Needs Assessment and that there are still edits that need to happen. She 
continued that it was found that a lot of people don’t know the breadth of what 
BPRW does as a whole, including recreation programs and hosting and 
supporting special events, and specifically noted that active aging and fitness 
recreational programs were lost after the reductions in force. Sauve called out 
the consultant’s great job comparing our system and Department to national 
standards – noting that BPRW does a lot of what is usually offered and then 
some unique areas, like Central Facilities, Urban Forestry, Conservation, 
community gardens, Urban Rangers, Cemeteries, beaches, a campground and 
marinas. She continued that there was a statistically valid survey collected in the 
Spring, which had over 400 responses, noting that 84% said quality of and access
to parks, nature and the lake are why they choose/choose to stay in Burlington, 
with quotes from outreach to support that data. Sauve then shared that overall, 
residents are very satisfied with the BPRW system, but they do feel that there 
are some gaps like indoor recreation and outdoor swimming areas (mostly due 
to cyanobacteria blooms that cause closures). She continued that when asked 
about barriers, most residents said that they do not know what is offered 
through BPRW, Burlington residents using facilities in other neighboring towns 
and safety/security concerns. The next section of the presentation focused on 
access to and supply of recreational amenities, with bathrooms, access to water 
and trails as the top priorities for people.  
Lewis noted that the consultants mentioned that some of the items in the lower 
priority sections are extremely important to smaller groups of people.  
Sauve continued by sharing a slide about how BPRW compares to cities of a 
similar size with outdoor amenities, noting that they perform well in all but a few 
like rectangular sports fields, diamond sports fields and standalone pickleball 
courts, which could be a challenge to meet.   
Etter asked about demand for field space and Sauve answered that there is a 
high demand, mostly for soccer field space. 
Sauve continued by touching on a slide about strengths and weaknesses that the 
Miller Recreation Center and Leddy Ice Arena have, noting the difficult set-up of 
the Miller Center which was originally built as an armory and that Leddy has an 
aging system with a lot of deferred maintenance. Shen then shared that supply 
does not necessarily indicate how accessible amenities are to residents in various 
neighborhoods by showing a map of Burlington with areas marked within a 10 
minute walk of a playground and then another map showing that a vast majority 
of residents live within a 10 minute walk of a park, but there are some areas with 
a higher local supply of parkland per resident than others. She continued by 
sharing an overlay map that will help guide where to concentrate on investments 
in the park system and amenities as well as adding parks based on community 
need, like in areas where new housing is going in. Sauve then touched on 
programming and special events, with more special events being a top priority 
for a majority of survey takers, closely followed by performing arts, fitness and 
wellness programs, nature programs, winter outdoor activities and adult 
programs. The next slide showed all of the programs that are offered through 
the Department, and 2 categories that were not offered in 2026 (active aging 
and adult fitness) due to the reduction in force, noting that prior to the rifs, 
BPRW offered programs in nearly every NRPA benchmark category. The next 
slide noted that 2 recent significant dips in programming were due to the COVID 
pandemic and staff reductions, with the peak in 2023 being over 400 programs 
and the low in 2026 being 181, but Sauve noted that with the Rec team being 
fully staffed up again the hope is that that number will increase again in 2027.
Lantieri asked for confirmation that rec programming is typically revenue 
positive, noting that if that was the case then it would be less financially viable to 
not have these programs.   
Sauve answered yes. She continued that even though there have been less 
programs, registration for the existing programs has increased. She continued by 
sharing a slide showing the typical timeline for programming and events 
throughout the year, noting that most happen between May and August. The 
next set of slides in the presentation focused on climate change, noting the 
increase in temperature over time in Burlington, less snow, more flooding, an 
increase in cyanobacteria blooms and a heat map of the City with the hottest 
area being downtown because there is less tree canopy and opportunity to 
increase that. Sauve continued by sharing a map of the tree canopy in 
Burlington, noting that it is related to heat reduction, stormwater capture, 
beauty and other benefits and that there was a goal in the 2015 plan to reach 
50% tree canopy and we’re currently at about 40%. She then shared a slide 
about the 2025 Open Space Plan, which established a framework for conserving, 
managing and expanding open space across the City. The next set of slides Sauve 
reviewed were focused on budget and staffing assessments and analyses, noting 
that BPRW needs a large budget because they oversee a lot of things, which is 
why there has been a 44% increase in the budget since 2015 (with the 
adjustment due to inflation being 5.9%). The next slide showed that BPRW’s 
capital spending in 2024 and 2025 was very low compared to comparable 
agencies nationwide. Sauve continued that earned revenue and special taxes 
make up the majority of the Department’s revenue, however earned revenue is 
not retained but instead returned to the general fund. She then shared that 
BPRW’s earned revenue and cost recovery percentage are high compared to 
other agencies, with other agencies typical retaining about 20% compared to 
BPRW’s 0%.   
Lantieri chimed in that when he asked the lead consultant what was the most 
surprising finding, he said it was this.  
Sauve continued by sharing that most of the Department’s revenue comes from 
the Waterfront Division and Recreation programs and facility rentals. 
Mamo asked if it was too soon to tell if the reductions in force in the Department 
had resulted in a decline in revenue. 
Sauve answered that because they don’t have the 2026 information yet, when 
the drop in programming really happened post-rifs, it is hard to say at this point, 
but there’s a good chance that will be reflected in the data. The next slide Sauve 
shared was a timeline of all of the various plans BPRW has completed since 2012, 
noting there have been a lot! She then shared the final slide, which was the draft 
vision for the future based on the Needs Assessment and public engagement.
She noted that it is long, but also trying to touch on everything without being too 
specific. 
Mobley shared her relief and appreciation that the plan has gotten to a 
substantial place in terms of naming the challenges and opportunities that BPRW 
has.  
Lantieri asked when the next major public input opportunity would be.  
Sauve answered that there will be online feedback opportunities soon based on 
the open house information and feedback and asked Commissioners to help 
spread the word when that happens.  
5. Standing Items 
5.1 Parks Foundation Update 
Lantieri shared that there hasn’t been a meeting since the last Commission 
meeting, but there is a gathering happening soon to share knowledge about 
getting the next campaign off of the ground. 
5.2 Director’s Report 
Lewis pointed Commissioners to the Monthly Report. He then shared that they 
are about to enter into budgeting season and he will have more information on 
that at future meetings. He continued that colder weather is coming which 
means emergency cold weather shelter operations at the Miller Center and the 
potential for unexpected closures of the building for regular programming, but 
the Mayor is actively working on finding a permanent location for a winter 
shelter. Lewis then shared that the new Police Chief is now officially in command 
and will be touring the NPAs and joining the Mayor at upcoming meet-ups. Lewis 
also shared that the REIB committee is having an ongoing conversation about 
youth programming and how to engage the community better. He continued 
that they have asked for Department representation at their November 17th 
meeting to provide an overview of current programming challenges and 
opportunities. 
5.3 Commissioner’s Items & Volunteer Hours 
Davis shared that she went to the Plan BTV2050 open house and has continued 
her regular visits to Battery and City Hall parks. She had 1.5 hours to report.  
Mamo shared that he also attended the open house, where he shared he was 
approached by a City Councilor about the Vegetation Ordinance the Commission 
passed because the Ordinance Committee would be voting on that next week, 
and participated in the Leddy tree planting. He had 3 hours to report. 
Etter also attended the open house. 
Lantieri shared that there would be a clean-up of the Englesby Brook this coming 
Sunday, the Baird work day and Leddy tree planting were both successful and he 
attended the open house. He had 20 hours to report. 
Boehm shared that she also went to the open house. She had 2 hours to report.
Mobley shared that she also attended the open house and gave kudos to all 
involved, and she attended the Baird work day. She had 5 hours to report. 
Bergmann didn’t have any hours to report. 
6. Adjournment 
6.1 Motion to adjourn 
Boehm made a motion to adjourn, Bergmann seconded.  
All were in favor, none opposed.  
The meeting was adjourned at 7:02pm.
